stories.title: UK and EU agree draft deal to scrap Brexit red tape over food exports
stories.summary: The food deal, ahead of a UK-EU summit later this month, is the most significant part of the so-called Brexit reset agreed so far.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 3 November 2026

The UK and EU have agreed a draft deal on removing post-Brexit checks from food and agriculture exports, ahead of the UK-EU summit later this month.

The BBC understands the 200-page draft text for this so called "SPS" [sanitary and phytosanitary] agreement has been circulated to EU nations in Brussels for consideration at a meeting on Wednesday.

Similar texts for deals on emissions trading and a youth travel and work scheme have also been circulated alongside a 15-page draft joint statement for UK and EU top leaders.

The food deal is the most significant part of the so-called Brexit reset agreed so far, removing checks and red tape that hit exporters after the UK exited the EU's single market.

As a result of the agreement, the government claims the UK economy will eventually see £5.1bn worth of annual benefits.

Speaking during the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (Chogm) in Antigua and Barbuda, the prime minister said a UK-EU deal could add up to 0.4% extra on GDP.

The deal could have the following impact:

Exports to the EU of fresh sausages, burgers, shellfish from domestic waters and seed potatoes would be able to resume

It should remove the need for £200 Export Health Certificates, which confirm the product meets the health requirements of the country it is heading to

It should also end the need for £25 Phytosanitary certificates, which show that plants or plant products are free from pests and diseases

Inspector fees, organic certificates, some port fees and other checks for exports and imports to and from the EU could be removed

It will bring back passports for British pets being taken into the EU

In return, the UK is expected to commit to observing and adapting to existing EU regulations on plant, animal and food trade standards - a process called "dynamic alignment".

Each of the elements on the table was up for discussion under Sir Keir Starmer, and the summit would have taken place by now had Labour not replaced its leader in July.

Under Andy Burnham, Britain's approach to post-Brexit relations with the EU have shifted significantly. Sir Keir said the UK would not rejoin the bloc in his lifetime, while Burnham has said he would like to see Britain back in the EU in his.

At Chogm on Tuesday, Burnham said: "I think people in Britain would expect me to take that with both hands, given where we've been in recent times, and that's what I'm doing."

Pressed on whether it would be acceptable for the UK to have its rules on food trade made by the EU, he said: "We're not in the EU, therefore we do have to work with them in a different way.

"But if that can get growth, if that can help our farmers, if that can remove red tape from British businesses, I think most people would expect me to go to that summit and negotiate the best deal that I can.

"And that's what I've been doing in recent weeks, leaning in, being positive, having a really constructive relationship with our European partners and hopefully we can land a good deal for Britain in terms of growth but also I hope more collaboration on controlling immigration."

Jon Walsh of Bio&Me said his firm had stopped exporting yoghurt due to vets' fees

Jon Walsh, the chief executive and co-founder of Bio&Me, which makes granolas, mueslis and yoghurts, told BBC 5 Live the draft deal sounded like "really good news".

"We're just a small company but when we were trying to export our yoghurts before, every time we'd send a pallet we had to pay a vet to inspect it and that was £140, and that meant that you'd lose money... so we had to stop."

The company also had problems exporting granola and overnight oats, with some shipments being returned.

"It was so frustrating because it was the same person filling out the same form and yet half would make it through and half wouldn't," Walsh said.

"You just kind of give up because you're losing money."

In an interview with ITV, Burnham said "public opinion has changed nationally" since the 2016 Brexit vote, but added he would "not run ahead of public opinion" on the issue.

"The public need to be the boss when it comes to whatever happens with Brexit," he added.

Burnham also said he had not proposed the return of freedom of movement between the UK and EU.

Asked by the BBC about the UK's relationship with the EU, Tory Leader Kemi Badenoch said that while we should "work closely", "dynamic alignment" with the EU would be a red line and "actually take us backwards".

Liberal Democrat Europe spokesperson Al Pinkerton said the draft deal was a "patch, not a fix".

"The real solution is to rejoin the single market and to establish a customs union with the EU," he added.

Reform UK's business spokesman Richard Tice said: "One of the key benefits of Brexit was that Britain no longer had to adhere to ridiculous EU rules.

"Returning to any form of alignment with Europe would crush Britain's competitiveness and force us to surrender sovereignty over trade policy, putting trade deals worth hundreds of billions of pounds at risk."

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen with Prime Minister Andy Burnham

While UK rules remain mostly aligned with EU ones, there are some areas where England has diverged from the EU rule book, for example on "precision breeding" of plants, previously known as gene editing. In recent weeks, agreement has been struck on transition arrangements while the EU's new regulations come in to force.

The government has already announced a European Partnerships Bill which will provide a legal mechanism for the application of new EU rules and regulations. This will also allow for the necessary alignments for the linking of the UK emissions trading scheme with the EU's, and save the need for UK exporters to pay the EU's new carbon border tax.

The draft agreements will be discussed at a meeting of EU ambassadors called Coreper on Wednesday, with some key details on the planned numbers in a Youth Experience Scheme to be finalised at a political level in the coming days. A discount on full foreign student fees for EU students is likely to be pushed to next year alongside a plan to reconnect electricity markets.

The BBC understands the draft agreements will also include some references to UK involvement in defence co-operation schemes, access to law enforcement databases and some reassurances over the EU's "Made in Europe" plans .

A food deal will have particular significance for Northern Ireland, radically reducing the impact of the post-Brexit Irish Sea border.

Northern Ireland's Brexit deal kept it inside the EU's single market for goods. That means food products from elsewhere in the UK require paperwork and some physical checks when arriving at NI's ports. A deal will ultimately end those requirements.

While the food trade plans have been backed by supermarkets and farmers representatives, some pro-Brexit campaigners have criticised the reapplication of EU rules. The post-Brexit trade deal signed by Boris Johnson's government prioritised regulatory freedoms for the UK over avoiding new regulatory red tape, checks and delays.

But William Bain, the British Chamber of Commerce's (BCC) head of trade policy, told the BBC's Today programme that business overall thought it was a "price is worth paying" to follow common rules, as companies would benefit from "lower costs, reduced delays [and] increased market access".

At the moment, he said, the requirement for Export Health Certificates can add thousands of pounds of costs to each truck carrying goods, in addition "to the delays that people find at the ports or at the borders".

"So we get lower exports because of the delays and the massive increases in costs that have come into the supply chain."

The BCC has released a new analysis of its members' views suggesting options for a closer relationship.

The business lobby group says the current trade relationship is "failing to deliver", leaving firms "struggling with a thicket of Brexit red tape" nearly six years after the UK's exit from the bloc.

Watch: King says slave trade a 'shameful chapter' that 'fills my heart with horror'

Published 3 November 2026

King Charles has described the transatlantic slave trade as a "shameful chapter of history" that filled him with "profound sorrow" as he opened a summit of Commonwealth leaders in the Caribbean.

He said the trade in enslaved persons "still casts a shadow" over the association of nations.

There have been calls from some for the UK to make a formal apology for its historic role in the slave trade ahead of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (Chogm) in Antigua and Barbuda, but there was not one in the King's address.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham, also at the summit, has said that he is open to Britain issuing a formal apology but has ruled out financial reparations.

While there was no direct apology, the King did offer some contrition - and there was also an acknowledgement that he had personally learnt more about the legacy of the slave trade.

He said: "The transatlantic trade in enslaved persons still casts a shadow over these islands and other members of our Commonwealth.

"As I have said before, that shameful chapter of history is one that fills my heart with horror and my soul with the most profound personal sorrow."

He told the summit: "The more I have furthered my own understanding of the issues, through listening, learning and looking, the more committed I have become to finding ways for us to work in modern partnership to address the wrongs of the past with action for the future."

King Charles continued: "History is not ours to choose or to change. It is bequeathed to us in complex synthesis by forebears we can never know.

"Our inheritance includes both their achievements and their failures – the good they did as well as the wrongs."

The King's address also referenced the "brutal conflicts" the world is facing, the "catastrophic reality" of climate and rapid technological development.

The Chogm meeting gathers leaders from 56 states every two years in a different part of the Commonwealth, a voluntary grouping made up primarily of former territories of the British Empire.

The biennial meeting's official theme this year is Accelerating Partnerships and Investment for a Prosperous Commonwealth.

Speaking on Tuesday, Burnham said his government was bringing a new approach, aiming to "revitalise the Commonwealth", despite turning down demands for reparations.

"I've been very clear that we do not support reparations," he said.

"But it's not the case that we don't support countries in the Commonwealth around development, and helping them with debt issues that they've got, green finance.

"That's what we've done under all governments and in my view we should continue to do as part of being a Commonwealth."

The King and Queen are on a tour of the Caribbean which has reignited difficult debates over the UK's colonial legacy in the region.

On his first stop in the Bahamas, the King delivered a speech in which he spoke of the "suffering of the past".

In Guyana, he visited the site of a Slave Rebellion, where hundreds of enslaved people were killed.

Plaid and Labour previously failed to agree on spending on support for children with additional learning needs

Published 3 November 2026

The Senedd has passed the Welsh government's mini-budget, nearly four months after the original version was defeated, following a deal between Plaid Cymru ministers and Labour.

Under the agreement, announced in October , an extra £60m will be spent on supporting children with additional learning needs (ALN).

Labour, now in opposition after heavy election losses , had rejected a £40m package spread over three years in July, with leader Ken Skates demanding £100m this financial year instead.

By voting for the extra spending plans on Tuesday evening Labour gave the minority Plaid government the numbers it needed.

Plaid Cymru's original mini-budget also included £100m for the NHS to bring down waiting times, £55m for childcare and £40m for school repairs, spending that can now go ahead.

Former Welsh Labour leader Mark Drakeford previously said his party had made mistakes in its summer negotiations with Plaid, and suggested there was a case for accepting the money previously offered by the government.

First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth agreed his government had learned lessons from its failure to reach a deal in July.

Finance Minister Elin Jones began the debate "by recognising the constructive discussions that have taken place in recent weeks with the Labour group".

On ALN, she said: "While there have been differing views on how best to respond there has been a broad recognition that these pressures are real and require action. That shared understanding has enabled agreement to be reached."

Reform's finance spokesperson, Cai Parry Jones, criticised Labour for "somehow backing this budget" despite the NAHT teaching union being in dispute with the government.

"Ken, who is really pulling the strings in Welsh Labour?" he said, suggesting Mark Drakeford's views on the budget may have been influential behind the scenes.

He called for foreign spending to be cut back.

Huw Thomas, Labour's finance spokesperson, said the process of agreeing a supplementary budget had been more difficult than it should have been.

But he said Plaid had seemed to have learned "lessons", and Labour had secured 50% more on ALN than Plaid Cymru had put on the table in the summer.

Calling for the money to be made available as soon as possible, he said: "Schools cannot afford lengthy delays and bureaucratic obstacles."

Welsh Conservative Peter Fox said: "We were told a Plaid Cymru government would be different,", confirming his party would vote against the budget.

"The budget just seems to be business as usual wrapped in different colours."

The budget motion was passed in the Senedd with 54 votes in support and 39 against.

European shares power ahead; bond yields decline

European shares are powering ahead! The FTSE 100 index in London has surged 207 points to 10,845, a near-2% gain.

The Dax in Frankfurt is up by a similar amount, while the French and Italian markets have jumped more than 2% and the Spanish index has soared 3.2%.

The pan-European Stoxx 66 has gained 1.8%.

Banking and clean energy stocks were among the top gainers, while defence stocks fell sharply both sides of the Atlantic (including in US pre-market trading), as Trump’s $1.5 trillion budget request for the Pentagon is likely to face far more scrutiny in Congress. The UK’s BAE Systems , which relies on the US for almost half its revenues, fell almost 6% earlier and is now down nearly 2%.

Wall Street is expected to open higher in less than half an hour, after Democrats secured sweeping victories in the midterm elections and secured control of US Congress Investors are hoping that it will be able to limit Donald Trump ’s scope for abrupt policy shifts, and keep a lid on government spending and borrowing.

The yield, or interest rate on the benchmark 10-year UK gilt is down 6 basis points at 5.18%, while the corresponding US Treasury yield has fallen 5.1bps to 4.91%.

Oil prices are down sharply , easing inflation fears, with Brent crude falling towards $100 a barrel. It is currently trading $2.72 a barrel lower at $100.87 a barrel, a 2.67% decline, as markets await Washington’s next move against Iran.

Eurozone yields nudged higher after inflation in the eurozone hit 4% last month, the highest in three years, and up from 3.8% in September.

The core inflation figure, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, remained at 2.5%, also in line with economists’ expectations, according to the flash estimate from the eurozone’s statistics office Eurostat.

The dollar slid 0.5% against a basket of major currencies, driven by expectations of more regulation of the booming AI sector, which could lead to slower economic growth.

Spot gold , seen as a safe haven investment, jumped 2.9% to $4,041 an ounce.

Here’s our full market story.

Closing summary

On Wall Street and in Europe, stocks are powering ahead after Democrats won control of US Congress. The Dow Jones gained 2.5%, the benchmark S&P 500 rose 1.5% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq climbed 2.5% (overnight, stock futures initially fell sharply but quickly reversed those losses).

You can follow the latest midterm election news here:

Big technology companies such as Amazon and Google owner Alphabet have jumped while shares in Elon Musk ’s Tesla and SpaceX slid. Musk spent nearly half a billion dollars backing Republican candidates, including in Texas, the home state of both companies.

AI stocks such as CoreWeave and datacentre operators tanked on the prospect of tighter regulation of the sector.

The FTSE 100 index in London climbed more than 200 points to 10,845, a near 2% gain. The pan-European Stoxx 600 was also up 1.96%.

US, UK and eurozone government bonds rallied , pushing yields lower. The yield, or interest rate, on the benchmark 10-year US Treasury fell 4.6 basis points to 4.90%.

The yield on the 10-year UK gilt slid 8.7 basis points 5.15% while that on equivalent Italian bonds dropped 9.5bps to 4.36%, and the German yield, the benchmark for the eurozone, slipped 2bps to 3.29% – indicating easing borrowing costs for governments.

The dollar has pared losses and is now down 0.35% against other major currencies, after sliding 0.6% to a one-month low overnight.

Spot gold jumped 3% to $4,047 an ounce. In oil markets, Brent crude fell towards $100 a barrel, losing more than $3 a barrel, or 3%, at one stage. It is now down 2.7% at $100.83 a barrel, as as investors await Washington’s next move against Iran.

We are wrapping up for the day. We’ll be back tomorrow. Thank you for reading. Take care! – JK

Tesla, SpaceX and datacentre shares fall sharply along with defence stocks, while big tech stocks rise

Several big technology stocks rose: Amazon jumped 7.7%, Facebook and Instagram parent Meta Platforms rose 2.6% and Google owner Alphabet climbed 5.4%.

However, Elon Musk -led Tesla and SpaceX dropped 2.5% and 0.6% respectively. Musk spent nearly half a billion dollars backing Republican candidates, including in Texas, the home state of both companies.

Cloud computer company CoreWeave slid 4.8%. Datacentre operators IREN plunged 9.6%, Hut 8 slumped 15.7%, Applied Digital Corporation lost 4.8% and Core Scientific slid 10.8%.

The AI trade will be in focus for a while, after Democrats won governorship races in key datacentre states Texas and Georgia, where public opposition to sprawling, enegy-hungry datacentres has been growing. The new governor of Texas, Gina Hinojosa , has repeatedly called for a moratorium on new datacentres.

Among chipmakers, shares in Advanced Micro Devices rose 1.4% after it forecast faster than expected growth next year.

Defence stocks have taken a hit on both sides of the Atlantic as Donald Trump ’s $1.5 trillion Pentagon budget request now faces a bumpy ride through US Congress. US stocks Northrop Grumman , RTX Corporation and Lockheed Martin fell 3.5%, 3.6% and 5.1% respectively. In London, BAE Systems is down 2.5%.

The dollar has pared losses and is now down 0.3% against other major currencies, after sliding 0.6% to a one-month low overnight.

Rachel Winter , partner at Killik & Co, says

double quotation mark The market is experiencing a sizeable post-election bump, thanks to the removal of the pre-election uncertainty and the fact that Donald Trump has not contested the result. Ordinarily, a divided government is preferable for the markets, as the associated gridlock makes big legislative changes less likely. However, while the Democrats have won control of both the House and the Senate, Trump is now referring to himself as ‘Mr Veto’, which implies that a state of legislative gridlock will likely endure for the remainder of his presidential term. The past few trading sessions have been characterised by a rotation out of tech and into other sectors as the Democrats advanced in the polls. Several polls have indicated that Democratic voters are more likely to oppose data centres, and new Democratic senators have been elected following campaigns that focused on greater restrictions on data centre construction. This is potential a problem for a variety of companies in this space, most notably CoreWeave, Oracle , SpaceX and Tesla. Texas had accounted for over a quarter of planned data centre capacity, and some of this could now be at risk, particularly for Elon Musk, who selected Texas as the home of his business empire. With the new Texas Democrat James Talarico now in the driving seat, backed by a campaign platform supporting greater data centre regulation, all eyes will be on his next move. Democratic control of Congress will make further conflict with Iran more difficult, which has likely driven the drop in Brent crude, as the world hopes for an easing of oil supply concerns. This should also be helpful in terms of bringing down inflation. With a prolonged conflict now harder to maintain, defence spending is less likely to rise, which has put both BAE and Northrop Grumman in negative territory.

Wall Street opens higher after Democrats secure Congress

Wall Street has surged at the open, after Democrats scored historic victories in midterm elections and secured control of US Congress.

The Dow Jones rose 2%, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq and the benchmark S&P 500 both gained more than 1%. That’s quite a reversal: Overnight, stock futures fell sharply as investors worried about the prospect of tougher regulation of the AI sector and the impact on economic growth.

However, Michael Heydt , senior vice president and sector lead of global sovereign ratings at Morningstar, voices a note of caution.

double quotation mark The central consequence of Democratic control of Congress is likely to be gridlock rather than sweeping policy change. While Democrats may seek to advance healthcare, oversight, and affordability priorities, substantial legislative action will remain constrained by Senate procedures and presidential veto authority. As a result, investors should focus less on major tax or spending shifts and more on the risks associated with government funding negotiations, debt ceiling debates, congressional investigations, and confirmation battles. Although targeted bipartisan cooperation remains possible in areas such as permitting reform, energy infrastructure, and AI regulation, the next two years are more likely to be defined by institutional confrontation and political positioning ahead of the 2028 election cycle.

Here’s our full market story.

Ion Jauregui , market analyst from the UK-based brokerage ActivTrades, says the sharp decline in Nasdaq futures earlier was an overreaction, but they have since recovered strongly.

double quotation mark Although we know that having a Democrat-run congress will increase the likelihood of increased scrutiny for AI, data centres and increased investment into technology, this does not mean that there will be a significant reduction in spending. Big tech companies will be concerned about their valuations. People are beginning to question just how much they are investing in AI and how long until they see returns. Adding regulation concerns into the mix, this looks more like a re-rating. Big tech stocks, AI infrastructure, datacentre developers and some of the semiconductors are likely to be the most vulnerable to a Democratic Congress. Cryptocurrencies and some financial stocks are also likely to face a more difficult regulatory environment. Renewable Energy, Utility and clean energy investment companies may see benefits from the positive political environment. Healthcare is likely to be more of a mixed bag due to the impact of regulation on drug pricing and insurance. European clean energy and bank stocks have rallied on the result. However, for now, I would say that it is mostly a repositioning. Clean energy stocks are seeing benefits from the more positive political environment. European banks are also seeing benefits from increased risk appetite. However, this is based on expectations. To make this sustainable, we will need to see if there are real changes to fiscal, energy or regulatory policies due to the new political landscape in Washington.

Turning to the pound, which has gained 0.6% against the dollar to $1.3492 today, he said:

double quotation mark Sterling has gained significantly vs the dollar, nearing $1.35. This is largely due to the weaker dollar and lower US Treasury yields. However, interest rates in the UK will still be driven by domestic inflation and Bank of England policy. In terms of trade, having a Democrat-run Congress may limit further expansion in US fiscal policy but is unlikely to have a quick impact on the general protectionist approach.

George Saravelos , global head of currency research at Deutsche Bank, has sent us his thoughts on the midterm elections.

double quotation mark 1. Risk positive. We agree with the rebound in global equities and risky currencies overnight. The combination of a large Democratic majority in Congress and president Trump’s statement that he is willing to work with the opposition should act as a break on extreme policy outcomes and bring down risk premia. The market is increasingly likely to interpret surprising policy shifts from the executive as time-bound by the next presidential election or the new domestic political configuration. 2. No news is good news on Iran. Over the last 48 hours, president Trump stated that no attack on Iran is imminent and has acknowledged that the Iran war drove part of the election outcome. We have been writing that with oil flows through the Middle East having materially recovered, the market is pricing a large imminent risk premium of re-escalation and energy supply disruption. There is therefore negative time decay on the oil price, the more escalation is delayed, the bigger the downward pressure on oil. 3. All about the debt ceiling (and AI) now. The single biggest source of domestic policy uncertainty remaining in the US is the debt ceiling that will become binding by Q2 of next year. It is reported that Republicans aim to pass a debt ceiling increase via reconciliation over the next few weeks. If this succeeds, it will remove one additional layer of uncertainty on fiscal policy, while also preventing AI and other policy matters from getting bundled up in a protracted negotiation with a Democratic Congress. Irrespectively, question marks around the build-out of AI will likely persist. On balance, we see political developments overnight as supportive of a continued bottoming out in euro-dollar: lower energy and global policy risk premium but higher AI implementation risks should on balance weaken the dollar. If Congress fails passing a debt ceiling increase this year, we would consider it an added dollar negative.

Sterling hits seven-week high against dollar

Sterling has hit a seven-week high against the dollar, which weakened across the board following the mid-term election results.

The pound climbed 0.6% to $1.3495 earlier and is now up 0.5% at $1.3483. It also firmed slightly against the euro, to 83.43 pence.

Sterling is also underpinned by expectations of interest rate hikes from the Bank of England, which is expected to raise borrowing costs from 3.75% to 4% at its meeting tomorrow. Higher rates usually boost a currency because they lead to be better returns for investors.

Markets are expecting three more quarter-point rate hikes in the coming 12 months.

Cryptocurrencies initially fell but then recovered, after the Democrats won control of both houses of ⁠the US Congress in the ⁠midterm elections – seen as a potential ​blow to an industry that has sought faster deregulation for digital assets.

While Donald Trump has been championing reduced regulation, some Democrats have also backed a light-touch ⁠approach.

The crypto sector spent more than $300m backing crypto-friendly Democrat and Republican politicians during the current and previous election cycles, according to Reuters.

Bitcoin, the world’s best-known cryptocurrency, briefly touched a six-week low before recovering to trade 0.8% higher on the ⁠day at $78,460. This came after a reversal in the stock market, where US index futures were up 0.3%, having fallen as much ​as 2% at one point overnight. Ether gained 1.4% to trade ‌at $2,323.

Bitcoin has fallen around 41% ‌since reaching record highs above $122,000 in October 2025, taking the value of the broader crypto market to about $2.6 trillion, according to CoinMarketCap.

Arun Pillai-Essex , principal geopolitical analyst at the risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft, has looked at the impact on US trade policy .

He argues the US midterms point to a significant shift in the political landscape, with implications extending well beyond Washington. This is particularly the case for key trading partners and emerging markets in Asia, where US trade and technology policy has an outsized impact on investment and economic growth.

double quotation mark With affordability dominating the midterm debate, we expect growing bipartisan pressure for tariff relief, particularly from lawmakers representing agricultural states and areas with strong trade ties to Canada. We’ve already seen selective exemptions on Canadian imports ahead of the elections. We expect Congress to become more assertive on trade policy , challenging tariffs through disapproval resolutions and greater oversight. While presidential veto powers limit their direct impact, growing bipartisan opposition could raise the political costs of further escalation. However, we don’t expect a fundamental shift in the White House approach. Tariffs remain an important bargaining tool, and further duties targeting manufacturing overcapacity across 16 major economies remain likely, adding another layer of restrictions following the forced labour tariffs imposed earlier this year. The proposed overcapacity tariffs have a significant focus on Southeast Asia and the wider APAC region, adding to the trade pressures already facing regional exporters. A divided Washington is unlikely to offer much relief, with protectionist headwinds continuing to complicate trade and investment decisions across the region. Overall, we expect the broader tariff framework to remain largely intact, but with greater scope for selective exemptions and negotiated concessions, while the White House keeps the threat of further escalation on the table.

Turning to AI policy , he says:

double quotation mark Datacentre opposition cuts across party lines, driven by concerns over electricity, water and other local impacts. We’re already seeing this translate into state-level action, with New York and Texas moving to restrict new developments and growing scrutiny over who ultimately foots the bill. In a divided Washington, these concerns are likely to gain further political traction, particularly as both parties look to capitalise on public unease around AI. The debate over datacentres is increasingly feeding into a wider debate about the pace of AI adoption and its economic and social costs. However, we don’t expect the growing political backlash to significantly slow AI investment. Instead, developers are likely to face greater pressure to shoulder infrastructure costs, alongside tighter conditions on new projects. But the underlying tension isn’t going away. Washington wants to accelerate AI investment to maintain its technological lead, while state and local governments face growing pressure to protect households from high costs. At the federal level, a divided government will sharpen tensions with Congress and the White House over US tech policy. Two areas to watch closely are advanced semiconductor export controls and restrictions on outbound US investment into sensitive technologies. The central tension over semiconductor exports is between Congress pushing for tighter, legally binding restrictions and a White House seeking to preserve flexibility to negotiate, selectively ease controls and protect US commercial interests.

The Athenian led the people, he didn’t follow them, writes Prof Costas Milas

Your editorial ( The Guardian view on a changing Brexit debate: Kemi Badenoch is trapped in denial, 29 October ) notes that when it comes to Brexit, Andy Burnham appears to be following the voters. This, in my humble opinion, is a problem. Thucydides noted about Pericles, the Athenian statesman, that “it was he who led them [the people], rather than they who led him”.

It was arguably the constant and thoughtful guidance of Pericles to his fellow Athenian citizens that made Athens the dominant political and economic power, respected by its friends and enemies alike. Burnham needs to take the lead and show his cards on what type of relationship he wants to pursue with our European partners. To do so, he could start by asking the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) to produce an independent and authoritative analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of the different types of closer relationship with the EU.

The analysis should consider the potential impact of measures of UK economic policy uncertainty , which spiked during the Brexit referendum and remained notably elevated afterwards. The analysis should also model the very structural change currently taking place in the UK economy. Had there been no structural change (either abrupt or slow-moving), there wouldn’t have been any reason for voting in favour of Brexit in the first place.

The OBR has the knowledge and expertise to model the economic impact of the UK’s return to the EU. Burnham could then use the analysis to make his case to voters and lead the way, as Pericles would have done. Prof Costas Milas University of Liverpool

stories.title: What are the planned changes to immigration rules?
stories.summary: The home secretary sets out plans to change requirements for permanent settlement in the UK.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood set out the plans in the House of Commons

Published 2 November 2026

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has set out plans to overhaul immigration rules.

Proposals for stricter requirements to qualify for permanent settlement in the UK were first outlined in detail in November 2025, when Mahmood was home secretary in Sir Keir Starmer's government.

She has argued that settlement should be "earned", rather than being granted automatically, with those who contribute more to the country able to settle fastest.

Following a consultation , external , Mahmood has now announced her final decision on what changes should be taken forward.

Elements of her original proposals have been revised following a backlash from some Labour MPs, with plans to make foreign care workers already in the UK wait 15 years to qualify for settlement scrapped.

Mahmood scraps settlement plans for migrant care workers Published 1 day ago

Labour MPs pull their punches on immigration changes Published 1 day ago

What is settlement and indefinite leave to remain?

Indefinite leave to remain (ILR) – also known as settlement – gives someone the right to live, work and study in the UK for as long as they like.

Under the current system, people with ILR can also apply for benefits if they are eligible.

People who have lived in the UK for 12 months after being given ILR can apply for British citizenship, if they also meet other requirements , external .

How will the new rules affect migrants?

Under the government's plans, the standard length of time migrants will have to live in the UK to qualify for permanent settlement will double from five to 10 years.

Under this 10-year pathway, applicants must have earned at least £12,571 for five of the seven years immediately before being granted settlement.

However, there will be a shorter qualifying period of five years for certain groups, including:

People who earned at least £50,271 for three of five years immediately before applying for settlement

Care workers who earned at least £25,000 a year while meeting their visa conditions and arrived in the UK before May 2025

"Skilled" public service workers in health and education, such as doctors, nurses, teachers and social workers

Other health and education public service workers who fall below this skill level, for example nursing auxiliaries and teaching assistants, if they arrived in the UK before May 2025

People from Hong Kong who hold British National (Overseas) status

People earning over £125,141 a year, as well as "highly skilled" migrants such as those on Global Talent or Innovator Founder visas, will qualify after three years.

Migrants who have claimed certain benefits or breached immigration rules will only be able to settle after at least 20 years.

Adults with a criminal record will be refused settlement, with discretion to refuse cases where the offence was committed when the applicant was under 18.

To qualify for settlement, migrants will generally also have to meet other conditions, including:

Speak English to a high standard

Owe no debt to the government, such as unpaid taxes

Earn at least £12,571 a year for at least three years, aligned with the threshold for paying income tax

Some care workers will be able to qualify for settlement after five years

What about refugees?

There will be a different set of rules for refugees – people who have been granted asylum in the UK because they are unable to return to their own country as they fear persecution.

Refugees who arrived in the UK through an official government scheme will qualify for settlement after five years.

However, other refugees will need to wait 10 years and either work or study.

Those who do not work or study will need to wait 20 years.

Refugees who arrived in the UK by small boat or another illegal route will have to wait 20 years if they work or study, and 30 years if they don't.

Will migrants already in the UK be affected?

The changes will apply to migrants who are already in the UK but not those who have already been granted settlement.

What about family members?

A partner who arrives with someone who then applies for ILR will be able to settle at the same time, as long as they meet the relevant requirements.

However, a partner who joins later will need to complete the same qualifying residence period before they are eligible for settlement.

Eligible couples will be able to combine their earnings to meet the minimum income requirement.

The household income threshold will be £25,142 – twice the individual minimum income requirement.

Children under 18 will continue to be able to settle with their parents.

They will be exempt from the income, government debt, English language and Life in the UK test requirements, but will remain subject to the relevant suitability and criminality requirements.

Young adults aged 18 to 24, who remain dependant on their family, will also continue to be able to settle alongside them.

They will be expected to meet all the adult mandatory requirements but not the individual income requirement.

Someone who is aged 25 or over when their family becomes eligible for settlement will be expected to qualify independently.

Eligible partners, parents and children of British citizens will continue to qualify for settlement after five years.

stories.title: Mahmood refuses to put cost on care worker settlement climbdown
stories.summary: The home secretary says the full cost of dropping plans to extend the wait for settlement will be laid out in future.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood revised her settlement reforms after a backlash from some Labour MPs

Published 3 November 2026

The home secretary has declined to specify how much scrapping her plan to make foreign care workers already in the UK wait longer to qualify for permanent settlement will cost.

Shabana Mahmood had originally proposed doubling the wait from five years to 10 for most migrants, with some facing a 15-year wait, which the Home Office suggested could save £10bn.

But under revised plans described by the Tories as a "U-turn", some foreign care workers will continue to wait five years, and others will be able to seek a five-year extension.

While not detailing the cost of the revised plans, Mahmood told the BBC they would still save "billions" because workers in other sectors would have to wait longer.

In March, the Home Office said , external the net lifetime cost of care workers and their adult dependants expected to settle between 2026 and 2030 was estimated at £10bn under existing rules.

Mahmood was proposing to delay settlement for this cohort in response to concerns over record post-Brexit net migration figures under the previous Tory government - dubbed the "Boriswave" by critics.

She had previously argued that not delaying settlement for migrant care workers already in the UK would lead to a "£10bn drain on our public finances".

Following a backlash, Mahmood announced on Monday that care workers who arrived in the UK before May 2025 and earned at least £25,000 a year would continue to qualify after five years, alongside some other groups.

Foreign care workers who do not qualify for the five-year settlement will be able to apply for a new five-year visa, and then seek settlement.

Just over 500,000 people will now be delayed from gaining permanent residency, down from almost 800,000 before Monday's changes. Some 1.9m people will settle in the UK between 2026 and 2030, according to the Home Office.

Indefinite leave to remain (ILR), also known as settlement, gives a person the right to live, work and study in the UK for as long as they like and apply for benefits if they are eligible. They can also use it to apply for British citizenship.

No new cost figure yet

Asked about the cost of her revised plans, the home secretary told BBC Radio 4's Today programme the detailed costs would be published when her department puts the changes before Parliament.

In an interview recorded on Monday evening, she said the changes overall represented "savings in the billions" to the Department of Work and Pensions in people not claiming benefits.

"The reason for that is the cohort that was most likely to fall upon the state is that cohort of care workers not doing care work at the moment - if they'd settled at five years, many more of those would have gone on to claim benefits.

"That will now not happen because they will not be settling at five years - those individuals get a second chance to make that contribution that they originally came to make," she told Today.

The Home Office's £10bn figure was based on an estimate by the Migration Advisory Committee of how much an average migrant care worker would cost the UK in benefits and public services throughout their lifetime.

While Mahmood would not give a new savings figure, Home Office minister Anna Turley told BBC Breakfast it would be "at least £1bn over the next couple of years in terms of welfare savings" but "we'll be doing more calculations" on the total.

The Conservatives said the "U-turn" would cost the UK billions of pounds.

Most people who come to the UK do so legally, after being granted a visa before they travel.

A visa gives someone permission to enter or stay in the UK for a specific purpose, such as work, study or joining family members.

There were 727,487 people who came to the UK via visas from July 2025 to June 2026, not including visitors or people transiting through the UK. This was down by 15% on the same period the previous year.

That does not mean all those people travelled to the UK, only that they were approved to do so.

The most common type of visa people came to the UK on was study, which made up 53% of all visa entries from July 2025 to June 2026.

People from China were the most common group to come to the UK on study visas, making up 23% of the total.

Together, people from China and India accounted for nearly half of all study visas. This has been the case for many years.

The £10bn figure has been criticised by the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR), which found a £115bn addition , external to UK public finances under current settlement rules.

"Public debate has focused heavily on the costs of recent migration, but this is not the whole story," IPPR associate director Marley Morris said.

Mahmood also declined to say whether Prime Minister Andy Burnham had told her to change tack on her proposals, which she had put forward in November under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.

She told Today a public consultation had resulted in a "transformative package" that "strikes the right balance".

She has denied Monday's move was a U-turn, and said the revised plans meant some 500,000 people already in the UK would now have to wait longer than five years to qualify for settlement.

The exact wait will vary based on income and whether people arrived in the UK legally or illegally.

Mahmood had faced criticism within the Labour Party for proposing to retrospectively change the rules for migrant workers already in the UK.

Housing Secretary Angela Rayner had said it amounted to "chang[ing] the goalposts" , while several MPs described the retrospective approach as "un-British" and warned it could worsen the UK's skills shortage, particularly in the care sector.

stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Mayaya, once-remote, has become a hub for Chinese companies. But critics accuse them of exploitation and illegal exports

T he pork belly hits the oil with a sizzle, and a rich aroma of soy sauce and caramelising sugar fills the kitchen. Zhang Changchun, a middle-aged man from China’s Heilongjiang province, is cooking dinner for his friends on a warm evening in Mayaya, a small town in the Bolivian Amazon.

“Bolivia is my happy place,” he says in Mandarin as he adds the dish to a table overflowing with pork trotters, duck wings and braised sábalo fish. In this small restaurant, a group of half a dozen Chinese men gathers most nights to eat, drink and play mahjong.

Each man plays a critical role in the town’s booming gold business. Some work as investors or miners; others import supplies and equipment. Together, they run most of the town’s mining operations: about 20 open-pit mines and 12 dredge boats, operated by about 2,000 Bolivian and 200 Chinese workers.

The table gets rowdy as the men debate their afternoon games over high-end Chinese cigarettes and Bolivian beer. Almost every conversation revolves around money.

In less than a decade, private Chinese mining companies have turned this once-remote Amazonian town into a hub of gold speculation. Mining equipment stores, hotels and Chinese restaurants now line the main street.

“We developed this town,” Zhang says between gulps of beer and bites of pork. “Without the Chinese, there would be no Mayaya today.”

As record gold prices drive Amazonian deforestation and violent conflict, these small-scale, private mining operations are tightening China’s grip on the world’s gold reserves. The Guardian spent five days with Chinese miners, investors and traders.

The Bolivian Amazon has long attracted foreign capital, from rubber and timber industries to North American mining companies in the 1950s. But now, Chinese mining is defining a new era of extraction, as a global network of goods, machinery and labour often thrives illegally under Bolivian law.

A 2014 national law limits mining rights to cooperatives and independent miners, state-controlled firms and domestic and foreign private companies. Such foreign firms must have a registered Bolivian office and operate in their own name. The state permits joint ventures, leases and risk-sharing agreements between foreign and national firms, but only through public-private contracts, in which the state is a shareholder.

Chinese mining firms operating outside this framework act unlawfully. Under a 2016 law , cooperatives also risk expropriation if they contract, lease or share mining-concession risks with foreign firms.

C hinese goldminers first arrived in Mayaya in 2005, but it was in 2017 that a major wave of immigration took place, after China’s national development and reform commission banned domestic small-scale gold mining , citing environmental and national defence concerns. The crackdown sent many miners and investors searching for work globally, and spurred several companies to hire workers from mines closed back home to work at newly opened operations in Bolivia.

One of those firms is Shenzhen Vicstar Import and Export, which has operated in Bolivia since at least 2011. Officially, the firm does not carry out mining operations, listing only print materials and manufacturing in a supplier directory.

Campaigners say these companies skirt the law, “hiding behind” cooperatives to operate in Bolivia’s mining industry. On paper, foreign investors sign service contracts with local cooperatives, provide capital and machinery. In reality, they control the mines end to end, selecting sites, hiring workers, providing machinery, exporting gold and taking 75% to 80% of profits, says Alfredo Zaconeta, a mining researcher at environmental thinktank Cedla .

Behind these contracts, Zaconeta adds, Chinese investors evade legal responsibilities as the state lacks the resources and political will to oversee the mining lobby. He says it rarely, if ever, enforces existing ownership and permit rules.

As a result, in Bolivia, an entire economy has emerged to serve this migration, from La Paz lawyers specialising in Chinese work visas to a local phone store that doubles as an informal bank for exchanging bolivianos and renminbi. In some regions, Chinese miners recruit friends and family, forming home town clusters dedicated to the local mining industry.

Along Mayaya’s main street, shops sell all things Chinese – from bottled tea and cigarettes to pork intestines. Yang Yanbin, a Chinese investor, says: “As long as you have money to invest, this country welcomes you. We stuff all the money straight into our pockets.”

Chang Yuequan, a lifelong miner who has mined gold along the China-Russia border since his teens, is another Chinese investor in Mayaya. In 2017, after verifying Mayaya’s gold quality, he ordered 120 shipping containers from China and began assembling machinery.

In 2025, he opened his newest mine next to the Kaka River, which he named “Passion Fruit” in Spanish, referencing the wild vines covering the hillside. On one of his periodic visits, Chang and a Chinese employee watched an excavator in a huge pit claw soil into a loader before Bolivian workers blasted it with high-pressure hoses.

Chang says the workers then mix the slurry with mercury, then burn it to produce the final product: large, lumpy gold nuggets. Turning to the mine’s Chinese manager, Chang points to the green half of the hill and says: “This whole mountain is ours. Excavate that too.”

Chang’s friend and colleague, He Zijian, who ships gold from Mayaya to La Paz during price surges, confirms the Chinese influence in the region. He says: “Everything – down to the tiniest screws – is imported from China.”

The trade can be highly lucrative. Much of the gold from Mayaya ends up in Dubai via illegal exports. According to He, Chinese middlemen bring the bullion to Bolivia’s capital, La Paz, before smuggling it to the Gulf state. There, he says, the metal is sold at Murshid Bazar, Dubai’s largest gold market.

Gold in Dubai is often shipped further to Switzerland , where it is laundered into legal supply chains and sold in western markets. In July, police arrested a Bolivian man set to depart to Dubai from Santa Cruz, Bolivia. His four suitcases allegedly contained 189.5kg (418lb) of high-purity gold worth roughly £18.5m.

While the man arrested may not have links to Chinese mining companies, authorities say his arrest highlights the vast quantities of gold illegally exported from the country.

Jaime Sanabria, director of Bolivia’s mining regulator, Ajam , estimates that while Bolivia produces about 100 tonnes of gold a year, only about 10% is sold legally, costing the Bolivian government and the country’s people billions in lost revenue.

A longside illegal exports, the gold-mining boom has brought poor labour conditions and rapid environmental degradation. According to two dredge-boat miners, Bolivian workers are routinely paid a quarter of what Chinese workers doing the same jobs earn.

“They’ve left nothing for us,” says lifelong Mayaya resident Victoriano Piloy. “The money doesn’t stay here – that’s why we’re poor.”

In surrounding Indigenous communities, mercury poisoning has become increasingly common. Already hit hard by the climate crisis , deforestation and wildfires, residents often struggle to make a living through agriculture and fishing.

Many ultimately turn to mining, compounding mercury pollution. With Chinese companies controlling the river, Bolivian artisanal miners increasingly enter Madidi national park, one of the world’s most biodiverse. There have been tensions. In August, residents of a rural village south of Mayaya seized and burned mining machinery allegedly owned by a Chinese company, denouncing their environmental harms. Nearby municipalities have also banned gold mining .

“The environmental impact is devastating because no one is inspecting or enforcing the rules,” says Sanabria, the mining regulator, adding that about 80% of mining in the country is illegal.

While the government conducts environmental audits every year, Zaconeta says Chinese investors commonly receive advance notice and clean up before inspections. The decentralised nature of gold mining in Bolivia, with 3,117 cooperatives nationwide, complicates state regulation.

“It’s just a good faith declaration; it can’t be verified. Everyone knows they are breaking the law,” Zaconeta says.

The Ministry of Mining and Metallurgy did not respond to requests for comment. Shenzhen Vicstar Import and Export Co and the Regional Federation of Gold Mining Cooperatives of Bolivia were also approached for comments.

Despite the criticism directed at the mining industry, under the country’s new conservative president, Rodrigo Paz, the trend is toward even more permissive policies . In May, Paz signed an agreement with mining cooperatives that reduces barriers to mining in protected areas and Indigenous territories.

Yet, government incentives may not be enough to ensure foreign companies’ long-term presence in Bolivia’s mines. Chang Yuequan, one of Mayaya’s early Chinese investors, has spent his life chasing the world’s best gold from Russia to Tibet and North Korea, and finally into the Bolivian Amazon. Twelve years in, he knows Mayaya’s gold is depleting. He expects to move on to his next destination in five or six years – once his boats stop operating.

At least a dozen Paceña beers into one of the Chinese investors’ frequent dinners, one investor sums up their worldwide reach: “You’ll encounter Chinese people in every corner of the world.”

Then his friend jokes: “We are just powerful like that – we could conquer the world!”

stories.title: Labour MPs pull their punches on immigration changes
stories.summary: Angela Rayner previously said plans were "un-British" and ministers shouldn't shift "the goalposts".
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Shabana Mahmood has backed down on two elements

Published 2 November 2026

Today's announcement has long been viewed in government as a potential political banana skin.

When the home secretary announced her first version of changes to the settlement system last year, many Labour MPs, including the housing secretary Angela Rayner, voiced their concerns about the plans.

But there was a feeling that Sir Keir Starmer's government was determined to plough on regardless. Shabana Mahmood herself repeatedly expressed how important she believed the reforms were.

But the change of prime minister over the summer gave renewed hope to those unhappy Labour MPs that they could force the Home Office into two changes.

Firstly, social care workers – under the original plans many social care workers would have had to wait 15 years before becoming eligible for settlement.

Secondly, the retrospective nature of the plans – some MPs were uncomfortable at the idea of someone coming to the UK and expecting to be eligible for settlement after five years, but then having to wait longer.

Angela Rayner described that as "un-British" and said the government shouldn't be shifting "the goalposts".

She returned to the cabinet under Andy Burnham as housing secretary and chose to repeat those criticisms in an interview during the Labour Party conference in September.

That was seen as evidence that a debate inside the top levels of government about whether to water down the plans was well and truly rumbling on.

For all the Labour MPs who wanted a change, there were others, particularly those in Brexit-supporting areas, who wanted the home secretary to stick the course.

Some inside government felt nervous about providing what they saw as catnip to Reform and the Conservatives.

All of that added up to one of the more difficult decisions that has had to be taken since Burnham walked through the doors of Number 10.

In the end ministers chose to water down the proposals for care workers – those who arrived before May 2025 and earn at least £25,000 a year will qualify for settlement in five years.

But the retrospective nature of the plans, the thing Rayner described as shifting "the goalposts", hasn't changed.

Despite that, the majority of Labour MPs pulled their punches when Mahmood made a statement in the House of Commons earlier .

Perhaps the strongest pushback came from Rachael Maskell, who is no fan of the retrospective element - but others on the left of the party, including John McDonnell and Diane Abbott, were critical without being scathing.

Mahmood scraps settlement plans for migrant care workers Published 1 day ago

What are the planned changes to immigration rules? Published 1 day ago

Outside the Commons chamber, the mood among Labour folk was pretty similar to what was said from the green benches.

One would-be critic said that while they personally still had concerns about the plans announced today, they believed the Home Secretary had successfully taken the political sting out of the situation for now.

They said the campaign by MPs and unions had led to a "big win" on settlement for social care workers, but said they were still expecting to hear from constituents negatively affected by the new rules.

One Number 10 source praised Mahmood's "take no prisoners" performance in the chamber, argued she had "found the right balance" and said the announcement had gone down as well as could be expected with Labour colleagues.

Of course, the home secretary will still need to deal with criticism from other parties.

Her opposite number for the Conservatives, Chris Philp, accused Mahmood of a significant U-turn.

Philp highlighted a claim she had previously made – that allowing care workers to reach settlement more quickly could cost the UK £10bn.

The social care workers plans announced today will see around 500,000 people have their path to settlement delayed , that number would have been around 800,000 under the original plans last year.

In an interview with the BBC, Mahmood wouldn't say what sort of financial burden her watering down would result in.

She also refused to confirm whether Burnham had directly asked her to water down the plans.

They are tricky questions that she will have to navigate over the coming weeks.

But the general view within government is that this is one political hurdle that has been successfully jumped.

Published 4 November 2026, 00:03 GMT

Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds has met the US-based owners of Poundland as the government hopes to save the retailer from collapse.

The discount chain is on the brink of insolvency and Gordon Brothers, which bought it for £1 last June, has rejected a takeover bid which could have saved the 12,000 jobs currently at risk.

A meeting was due to be held on Thursday but has been brought forward as the scramble to secure a rescue deal for the firm intensifies.

Gordon Brothers has previously said Poundland faces multiple economic challenges from rising inflation, increasing staff costs, and "severe levels of shoplifting".

Both Reynolds and Prime Minister Andy Burnham have questioned why a deal for the future of the business has not been made.

On Wednesday, a source close to business secretary said Reynolds "has been firm that Gordon Brothers must do everything in their power to protect jobs and provide certainty for workers".

"He is pleased to have secured this commitment from Gordon Brothers in the meeting and will continue to hold the company to account and closely monitor developments," the source added.

It is understood that Gordon Brothers made a commitment in the meeting to prioritise bids that will protect workers and units.

However, it is still unclear whether the US investment firm will keep the business together or break it up.

Meanwhile, MPs say they have called in Poundland's owners for questioning on Wednesday 11 November to explain their role in the discount retailer's looming insolvency.

Liam Byrne, chair of Parliament's business committee, said: "Every report suggests Poundland is a viable, profitable business with a future ahead of it and without good reason to let it crash and burn - and then to break it up and sell it off piece by piece.

"We are asking Gordon Brothers to appear before Parliament to explain themselves and tell us just what it is that's preventing them from accepting the fully-funded deal on the table to save more than 12,000 jobs."

Business Minister Kate Dearden and union representatives met Poundland's managing director Barry Williams on Wednesday.

Mr Williams told the BBC that Poundland is profitable and sales were growing.

"We're back in profit and it has a bright future ahead of it if it's allowed to deliver that," he said.

Poundland has filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators, which protects it from its creditors until next Thursday.

Adam Turner: We would lose "a few million" if Poundland went under

Asked what his message for Poundland's owner was, Burnham said Gordon Brothers should "focus on the people in your employment" and "come up with a practical solution that saves jobs and saves those stores".

"There is a solution to be found here, sit down with us and let's find it," he added.

The meeting comes after a major Poundland supplier has said it will lose millions of pounds if the retailer goes bust.

Adam Turner, sales director at Bradford-based Highcrest Retail Brands, said Poundland was one of its biggest customers and its collapse would cost it "a few million" in lost sales.

The family owned business mainly sells confectionery to Poundland and turns over about £50m.

Turner said the firm becoming insolvent would leave a substantial gap in its balance sheet next year.

Highcrest was a "longstanding business that can stomach this", Turner said. But he warned other medium and small suppliers to the retailer have told him that "if Poundland goes under, so do they".

This echoes a warning from Poundland founder Steve Smith on Monday that two or three thousand suppliers to the firm, which only work for Poundland, would be directly affected by its collapse.

Not only would Poundland's 12,000 staff be affected in that case, but potentially up to 30,000 overall, he told the BBC on Wednesday.

He said he was "amazed" Poundland was being put into administration, pointing to the profitability of the company.

"Also, there's two offers on the table from some really good people," he added.

"All I'm asking is for Gordon Brothers to see if they can put a deal together."

Gordon Brothers said Walsall-based Poundland is "still not cash generative at a sustainable level" because of the economic issues it faces.

If Poundland's stores are sold to new buyers, some of the employees may get new jobs on the same premises.

However, it is understood that buyers are only interested in about half the stores at present – meaning roughly 6,000 employees would not be re-employed.

Poundland's founder offers to invest in firm Published 2 days ago

High stock levels

If Poundland goes under, suppliers will be getting "pennies in the pound" back from the administration, he said, which is "very upsetting" – although he still hopes a deal can be done so Poundland can remain solvent.

Poundland owners Gordon Brothers will be a secured creditor, which means they are first in line to get their money back, and suppliers "who have done nothing wrong" will take the financial hit.

"It's sad. It's a nightmare for us all to be honest with you. It's not just the suppliers, it's the staff at Poundland, some of these guys have been there for many years.

"It's from the warehouse staff all the way to the shop staff to everybody within head office. It's a massive ripple effect through the supply chain," he added.

Turner said he had no knowledge of whether Gordon Brothers had deliberately timed the process of Poundland going into administration so it could take advantage of having high stock levels, which it can then sell.

One of the ways Gordon Brothers makes money is through stock liquidations – selling off stock from collapsed businesses.

One insider familiar with the situation told the BBC that the timing of Poundland facing collapse was "odd" – most retailers don't fall over in the run-up to Christmas.

Ministers' questions

Dearden has said the government doesn't want to interfere with "current ongoing commercial negotiations", but that ministers want "clarity" on the plans for the retailer.

"It's absolutely legitimate for this government to ask the business if they're doing everything they can to protect employees and suppliers up and down the country," she added.

Dearden told MPs that the government would be ready to help the company's employees if Poundland collapses.

The head of Gordon Brothers' European operations reportedly told the government that the firm stood by its stewardship and had given Poundland £85m in additional financing since its purchase in 2025.

stories.title: People say they want small smartphones—the Enough Phone will put that to the test
stories.summary: It won't win the specs race, but it will actually fit in your hand.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
It won’t win the specs race, but it will actually fit in your hand.

The first modern smartphones had 3.5-inch screens, which can be hard to remember in today’s world of gargantuan glass slabs. Sure, people talk about wanting smaller phones, but will they buy one? Enough Phone is betting they will. The company will begin taking preorders for its first device today, which is built around a petite 5.3-inch screen that is apparently the smallest it could find with decent performance metrics.

The company’s cheeky name is reflected in its approach to phone design. A flagship killer this is not, but it’s probably “enough” for most people. It has a mid-range MediaTek processor, a single rear-facing camera, a polycarbonate body, and a fingerprint sensor in the power button.

With that compact screen, the Enough Phone will be dwarfed by almost every existing smartphone. While it’s a bit thicker, the device has almost the same footprint as the iPhone 13 Mini. Thinness takes a hit, as the designers have opted to make the battery user-replaceable. Like the Fairphone , you’ll just have to remove a few screws to get the back cover off.

On the software front, the device will offer a choice. You can get an Enough Phone with a standard Google-certified build of Android 17, which is probably what most people will choose. It also supports OdysseyOS , a streamlined, de-Googled version of Android that behaves like a dumbphone (it doesn’t even have a browser).

Some minor details are still up in the air. The designers aren’t yet sure about waterproofing and durability ratings, and the battery capacity could change. But they hope that spec will go up, not down, if it changes at all. Carrier support is also unclear right now. It will be an unlocked 5G phone, and the company is aiming for “broad global support.” But if you’re on a restrictive carrier like Verizon, you may be out of luck.

A waiting game

The other wrinkle is the timeline. The Enough Phone goes live on Kickstarter today , with shipping currently slated for May 2027. The phone might seem like enough today, but will you feel the same in six months? Plenty of Kickstarter projects have failed to deliver on time (or at all). The Enough Phone team points out that this isn’t its first smartphone effort, though. The team says it has designed and shipped hardware for other companies you’ve heard of, working as an original design manufacturer (ODM).

If you’ve been posting comments about how much you want a smaller phone, now’s your chance to do something about it. The Enough Phone starts at $399 for early backers. It will go up to $449 and then $499 later. The final MSRP will be $599. That’s not bad for a niche piece of hardware, given the rapid increase in component costs.

You will have to take a little leap of faith to get on board with the Enough Phone. The company says it plans to support the device with updates through 2032, which is almost flagship territory. But when a company like Samsung or Google makes that commitment, it’s essentially a guarantee. This is the first phone this group has made under its own brand, and there’s no telling how that will work out.

Watch: Key moments from the US midterm election results

Published 4 November 2026, 13:43 GMT

Democrat James Talarico's resounding victory in the Texas Senate race caused a major upset in the midterms for Republicans - and for Elon Musk.

According to the Financial Times , external , the billionaire's political action committee (Pac) contributed $47m (£35m) to Republican candidate Ken Paxton's campaign, on top of the $158m he gave the Senate Leadership Fund in September.

The money was not enough to stop the seat from turning Democrat for the first time since 1988. In his acceptance speech, Talarico said: "We just proved that all the money in the world is no match for the people of Texas."

"Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn't work this time," Musk jokingly wrote on X , external .

While stocks were broadly up on Wednesday morning following the election outcome, Musk's Tesla and SpaceX were down by 4.9% and 3.4% respectively. Many Democrats had been vocally outspoken against the expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) data centres on the campaign trail.

Democrats take control of US Congress as voters resoundingly reject Trump's Republicans

Talarico's victory marked a key turning point in the midterms, helping solidify the Democrats' control of the US Congress in a wave of wins across the US .

Musk has increasingly made Texas the hub of his companies, from Tesla's Austin headquarters to SpaceX's Starbase launch site.

As well as backing Paxton through outside groups, the X owner took to his own platform to spread conspiracy theories about the Democrat, posting: "There is something deeply wrong with Talarico" after he briefly disappeared from the campaign trail in October.

"There is something deeply wrong with a political system that allows one trillionaire to buy his own personal US Senator," Talarico posted in response.

On top of contributing to one of the most expensive Senate races ever, the SpaceX owner also became the top individual donor in this year's midterms overall , contributing an estimated $446m in backing Republican candidates.

Musk's money went through Super Pacs, groups which can raise unlimited sums but can't give directly to candidates or coordinate with their campaigns.

Individuals, parties and traditional groups face legal limits on direct donations.

Super Pacs get around this by spending independently, such as on ads backing a candidate.

Musk became one of the Republican Party's biggest donors in 2024, pouring hundreds of millions of dollars into Donald Trump's winning presidential campaign.

A similarly eye-watering amount was not enough to do the same for Paxton this time around.

stories.title: Binance says hackers who stole billions in crypto spent months planning heist
stories.summary: Techniques included laptop infections, compromised internal tooling, and fake job interviews.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Techniques included laptop infections, compromised internal tooling, and fake job interviews.

The hackers who stole billions of dollars in cryptocurrency from the Binance exchange spent months working on the theft and used both social engineering and novel malware in the process, the company said Tuesday.

The heist, which both the FBI and the TRM Security firm attributed to North Korean actors, initially targeted $6.34 billion in cryptocurrency from Binance wallets. The exchange has since frozen or intercepted $2.85 billion of that sum. Binance said it has set aside funds required to cover the loss and provided this link to a Proof of Reserves page. The $6.34 billion represents the biggest sum ever targeted in a cryptocurrency theft.

Advanced persistent threat

Binance said the people behind the heist began no later than June and continued until last Thursday, when they successfully compromised an engineer’s laptop and withdrew assets from several wallets. Like just about every organization that suffers a public, high-consequence hack, Binance said the threat actor was sophisticated and resourceful.

“Our current investigation indicates that this was a sophisticated, multi-stage campaign,” a report on the company’s investigation to date said. “It was not a single isolated breach or a simple phishing incident. The attackers combined a range of techniques, including social engineering by fake recruitment interviews, malicious software downloads, compromised internal AI tooling, endpoint compromise, and an advanced transaction-authorisation method.”

Binance said that the first incident related to the compromise likely occurred in June, when an engineer downloaded a tampered version of Homebrew. The company linked to this incident reported in May, and its security team detected the compromised laptop, but only after the malware operators obtained information about the roles of the engineer and his related colleagues on the Binance wallet infrastructure team.

In September, a separate engineer received messages through a legitimate job-hunting platform he was using. The message came from an individual posing as a project director looking to hire new employees. The purported project director arranged a first-round interview with a supposed HR representative and a second-round interview with the purported CEO of the fictitious company.

During the first interview, conducted over a video platform, the purported HR representative shared a social media account that included personal photos and videos. The second interview took place over a social chat app. During it, the engineer was instructed to download an “assignment” that linked to a code repository containing malicious code that eventually executed on the engineer’s device during the setup process.

“The malware employed sophisticated obfuscation and evasion techniques, including replacing a legitimate development tool component with a malicious version to execute commands and establish communication with an attacker-controlled external server,” Binance said. “The 0-day malware was not detected by the endpoint security protection tools at the time. The attacker also took steps to conceal the malicious activity and remove traces of the compromise, making detection and subsequent investigation more challenging.”

On October 20, the attackers used the compromised engineer’s computer and an internal AI tool to take control of two other engineer devices, including the one previously targeted with the trojanized Homebrew installer. That engineer’s wallet contained a token granting access to a container deployment.

Nine days later, between 17:15 and 19:56 UTC, the threat actor logged in to the third engineer’s device, used the stolen credential, deployed a container, and activated a script to initiate the transfer. Among other things, the attackers extended their unauthorized access to an internal wallet signing service to complete transactions outside the normal withdrawal process.

Binance continued:

Binance hot wallets on Solana and Optimism sent approximately 970,500 SOL and 44.2 million OP to attacker-controlled addresses. Binance then received an internal alert regarding large-volume transfers and immediately began investigating. Binance hot wallet sent 18,270 BTC to an attacker-controlled address. The attacker then used the signing service to exploit Ethereum’s EIP-7702 authorization mechanism. EIP-7702 allows an account to delegate certain execution rights to a smart contract without exposing the private key. In this case, the attacker used that mechanism to give an attacker-controlled smart contract partial execution rights over a Binance hot wallet. Binance immediately initiated multiple containment measures, including suspending withdrawals to restrict further outflows, coordinating with partners to freeze affected tokens, and taking steps to revoke unauthorized permissions. These efforts froze a total of $2.85 billion in assets. However, suspending withdrawals alone could not stop all unauthorized asset movements. The malicious EIP-7702 authorizations existed on-chain and operated independently of Binance’s normal withdrawal infrastructure.The attackers submitted 50 signing transactions to manipulate the account nonce and establish malicious delegation authorizations. Once established, these authorizations enabled the attackers to continue moving assets independently of Binance’s normal withdrawal infrastructure. Binance needed additional transactions to revoke these on-chain authorizations. The containment process involved additional technical complexities. Because the hot wallet used Multi-Party Computation (MPC), there was no single private key that could be used to immediately revoke the malicious EIP-7702 authorizations. The team therefore developed and executed a specialized procedure to revoke these authorizations, which required additional time. Furthermore, suspending withdrawals and shutting down hot wallet services did not automatically invalidate existing on-chain authorizations.

Separately, TRM Security said the attackers used various means to launder successfully transferred assets through the TRON and Ethereum blockchain networks. The methods included “a self-minted token and liquidity pool, a lending receipt token passed between wallets, and cross-chain swaps chained through two bridges.”

TRM is tracking the North Korean hacking group under the name TraderTraitor.
